transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2026-04-27 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Sarah Gomez (Atlas - ML Platform Lead), Devon Park (Atlas - Infra), Hannah Lee (Atlas - CTO)

Summary (auto): Quick optimize walkthrough focused on quantization options; discussed quality regressions, latency SLOs, and next steps for a pilot.

00:00:00 - Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate you carving out time. I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood team, joining with Liam who'll run through the Optimize quant profiles deep dive. Quick around the room?
00:00:14 - Sarah: Hey Maya, Sarah here, ML Platform Lead at Atlas. We're mainly interested in reducing inference cost while keeping accuracy for our document-parsing models.
00:00:22 - Devon: Devon, infra. We'll be owning the private deployment side if we go that route.
00:00:26 - Hannah: Hannah, CTO. I'll be around for high-level questions.
00:00:30 - Liam: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: show Optimize UI for quant profiles, go over INT8/FP8 quality vs latency dashboards, demo perf runs and logs, then discuss POC scope and security.
00:00:45 - Sarah: Sounds good. We're particularly worried about tail latency on shorter prompts, like 50-150 tokens, and whether FP8 introduces instability in hallucinations for financial jargon.
00:00:58 - Liam: Totally. We'll show both absolute token-level quality metrics and human eval examples. Note, small transcription heads up, sometimes our tool labels things weirdly.
00:01:14 - Maya: Alright Liam, take it away.

00:01:30 - Liam: Ok so first slide is the Optimize Quant Profiles view. You can see we have pre-configured profiles: fp8-balanced, int8-aggressive, int8-safe, and fp8-highperf. The idea is these map to different accuracy/latency pareto points; optimize suggests a profile per workload.
00:01:50 - Liam: On the left is quality delta vs baseline fp32, on the right is 95th percentile latency. For your document parsing workload we usually recommend int8-safe or fp8-balanced as starting points.
00:02:10 - Sarah: Quick question: how are you measuring quality delta? Is it token-level or downstream task accuracy?
00:02:18 - Liam: Good callout - we do both. The dashboard aggregates intrinsic metrics (perplexity/token-accuracy) and your supplied eval set for downstream metrics like entity extraction F1. In this demo I'm using a synthetic doc-extract eval to show the delta.
00:02:35 - Devon: Are those runs on dedicated infra or hosted? I want to understand if we'll see same numbers on our private cluster.
00:02:42 - Liam: These runs are on Redwood Dedicated in us-west g4-type infra for consistency; for private/on-prem we provide the same Optimize tooling and profile configs but kernel availability and quant runtimes can vary slightly - we'll include that in the POC.

00:03:05 - Liam: Now demoing a side-by-side inference trace: FP32 baseline vs INT8 vs FP8. Notice INT8-aggressive drops latency ~2.3x for small sequences but shows a small 1.5-2% hit on named-entity recall in the worst-case prompts. FP8-balanced hits more of the mid-ground - similar latency improvements with smaller quality delta for most prompts but occasional instability on rare tokens.
00:03:35 - Sarah: That instability on rare tokens - are we talking about numeric formats or domain-specific ticker symbols?
00:03:42 - Liam: Mostly domain tokens and rare encodings - dates, slashes, some special ticker punctuation. We use a calibration/quant-profile where we keep critical layers in higher precision if your eval set shows degradation. That's the int8-safe idea.
00:03:58 - Maya: Also worth mentioning cache behavior - KV/prefix caching maintains state so reusing prefixes often reduces effective latency and can mitigate some of the quality noise for repeated patterns.

00:04:20 - Devon: Could you show the latency tail chart? We're trying to get 95th < 200ms for single-turn responses under 150 tokens.
00:04:27 - Liam: Sure. For int8-safe on this hardware we see median ~60ms, 95th ~180ms with batch size 1 and an optimized kernel. FP8-balanced hits 95th ~160ms but with slightly wider variance in rare prompts. Important: sequence length and tokenizer differences matter; on longer sequences the delta tightens.
00:04:55 - Hannah: What about concurrency? Our throughput needs are modest, but we want predictable tail. How does batching affect these numbers?
00:05:05 - Liam: Batching increases throughput but can add headroom to tail latency. Optimize suggests per-route batching and dynamic batch thresholds - for sub-200ms SLOs we usually keep batching minimal and rely on kernel-level optimizations plus autoscaling. There's a toggle in the console to set max batch size for a route.

00:05:30 - Sarah: We also use strict audit logs and KMS for keys. Any concerns with quantized models plus KMS or private deployments?
00:05:38 - Maya: No impact; quantization is orthogonal to encryption at rest or in transit. For Private deployment we integrate with your KMS/HSM and we keep audit logs; SOC2 artifacts will be shared. Some customers prefer Dedicated with VPC peering to control egress.

00:06:00 - Liam: Back to quality: here's an example where INT8-aggressive produced a subtle paraphrase that changed a numeric amount - we flagged those via Optimize's QA rules. You can configure alert thresholds linked to prompt sets/evals so we trigger a regression alert if F1 drops or numeric tolerances exceed.
00:06:22 - Devon: How intrusive is the calibration step? We need to avoid long pipeline changes.
00:06:28 - Liam: Calibration is an offline step that runs on a representative sample - it takes a few hours for a 10k-sample on the Dedicated pool but we parallelize it. The output is a quant profile you can pin. It doesn't change your model code; it's a serving config.

00:06:50 - Sarah: For the POC, we'd like to see: (1) end-to-end perf on our prompt set, (2) quality metrics for NER and numeric extraction, (3) a cost estimate per 1M tokens for int8 vs fp8 vs baseline.
00:07:03 - Maya: Yep that's the typical POC ask; we'll include a cost model in the spreadsheet.

00:07:10 - Liam: Quick note on fallback: Optimize can route to a higher-precision variant automatically when a confidence threshold is low - e.g., if the model's logit gap indicates uncertainty we can route that single request to FP32 or a safe int8 variant to avoid bad outputs. That increases cost for that request but keeps quality.
00:07:32 - Hannah: Is that routing synchronous? Latency cost?
00:07:36 - Liam: We do synchronous fallback; the added latency is roughly a cold-call to the higher-precision path - usually +80-150ms depending on infra. You can tune the policy - for some customers we do background re-checks and send second-pass results async.

00:07:58 - Sarah: You mentioned kernel availability differences earlier. Could you explain what we might need on-prem?
00:08:05 - Liam: For FP8 we rely on newer GPU runtimes and some assembly-level kernels. On on-prem Nvidia cards you'll need drivers and a small runtime package we supply; for certain older cards FP8 may not have optimized kernels so FP8 might fall back to slower paths. We'll provide a compatibility matrix.
00:08:25 - Devon: Good, send that. Also curious about model size - our fine-tuned model is 13B, any special considerations?
00:08:30 - Liam: 13B is in the sweet spot - quantization gains are sizable, and int8-safe tends to keep some final attention layers in higher precision which helps preserve generation fidelity. We typically test layer-wise sensitivity during calibration.

00:08:50 - Maya: I'll share an example calibration report we've run for a 13B model; it's helpful to see layer sensitivity heatmaps.
00:08:58 - Sarah: Perfect.

00:09:05 - Liam: Demoing the live compare panel: you can upload your eval set, we show side-by-side outputs and a diff view that highlights token-level changes. Here you can jump to examples where FP8 changed a numeric token. You can also pin tokens to be preserved in higher precision via profile rules.
00:09:28 - Devon: That token pinning - does it require retraining?
00:09:31 - Liam: No, it's a serving-time rule. The runtime keeps those layers or embeddings at higher precision for matching tokens or token classes.

00:09:45 - Sarah: How do you surface regression alerts? Email, webhook?
00:09:50 - Liam: Both. Webhook, Slack, and in-console alerts. We can also tie alerts to automated rollbacks to previous profiles if a threshold is hit during a rollout.

00:10:05 - Maya: Quick public competitor note - some vendors push FP8 as always better; we recommend validated profiles and human evals. Fine to consider point solutions from Anthropic or OpenAI endpoints but they don't give the same dedicated profile control or private deployment parity.
00:10:25 - Hannah: Understood.

00:10:35 - Liam: Moving on to cost modeling: int8 typically reduces per-token compute cost ~40-55% depending on kernel efficiency; FP8 is in that same ballpark but can yield more variance. We'll attach your numbers to the spreadsheet for a more precise estimate.
00:10:55 - Sarah: We'll need cost per million tokens for cold and warm cache scenarios.
00:11:00 - Maya: We'll include both and show impact of caching and batching.

00:11:08 - Liam: Quick digression on SLO-driven routing: you can set per-route policies that prefer lower-cost variants but will route to higher-cost variants when latency or quality thresholds are at risk. That's how we hit customer SLOs without blowing up unit costs.
00:11:25 - Devon: For private deployment, is the Optimize agent something we host?
00:11:29 - Liam: The Optimize control plane can be either Redwood-managed or customer-managed - for on-prem we provide a control plane package that talks to a local agent. Data sent for evals is configurable - you can send hashes or anonymized payloads.

00:11:48 - Sarah: Ok next steps?
00:11:50 - Maya: Recap and actions: we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and calibration report, Liam will run extra FP8 vs INT8 runs on long-tail prompts, Sarah to send the sample eval set and SLO targets, and we'll schedule a POC kickoff.
00:12:05 - Hannah: Sounds good.

00:12:10 - Maya: Anything else?
00:12:12 - Sarah: One last thing - compliance wise, can you share any stuff around HSM/KMS integration and audit logs?
00:12:18 - Maya: Yep we'll share SOC2 docs and a KMS integration note as part of the security packet.
00:12:24 - Devon: Thanks everyone.
00:12:26 - Liam: Thanks, we'll follow up with the artifacts.
00:12:30 - End of meeting notes.

Call ended: 15:42 PDT
